title: Ambient and Autonomous Security: Building Trust in the Agentic AI Era

segments.text: >> ANNOUNCER: Please welcome Corporate
Vice President Microsoft Security, Vasu Jakkal.
>> VASU JAKKAL: Well, hello, hello, hello.
Good afternoon, everyone.
It's fantastic to be here with you all.
First, congratulations to Jen on her amazing CEO role.
Let's give it up for her.
That's amazing.
And then secondly, since we are all just separated by one
degree of freedom, I thought I'll start with
a little Footloose.
Just joking.
But I did want to start by wishing everyone at RSAC a
happy 35th anniversary.
Thank you, RSAC for your service.
Yes.
Thank you for bringing this incredible community together.
Thank you for your service.
It's invaluable and deeply appreciated.
Many defining moments in our industry have been ideated on
and discussed right here.
And when we look back 35 years ago to that first RSAC in 1991,
we can actually see that many of the forces shaping
today's world was set in motion that year.
In technology, the World Wide Web, who remembers that?
When public and information moved from closed systems to
globally accessible networks.
Linux was born, laying the foundations for open, scalable
computing and composable digital infrastructure,
and Windows-based computing was expanding rapidly,
signaling this upcoming workplace transformation.
The magnitude of what has changed between then and now
is hard to fathom, even for those of us living through it.
And if we could talk to those attendees in 1991, I'm sure they
would be probably shocked to know how many of us arrived
here today to Moscone Centre in a driverless car powered by AI.
They might be amazed to know that just a few miles
away from here, in UCSF, a neurosurgeon is working on
understanding tumors and removing the cells, the abnormal
cells at the margin of that tumor using AI.
And they might not even believe us if we told them
that agents would surface impactful vulnerabilities and
fix them autonomously.
It would sound like science fiction, and yet,
we know that that is true and happening today.
Organizations are becoming frontier where humans and
agents are working together, and we are only just scratching
the surface of AI.
But as always, with the case of technology advancement,
there will always be those who will use it
for nefarious purposes.
And today, we are at an inflexion point with the early
use of AI-powered attacks.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed that most malicious
user of AI today centers on improving the
threat actors' tradecraft.
Threat actors are using GenAI to draw phishing lures,
generating and debugging malware and scaffolding
scripts and infrastructure.
We've seen this in operations by North Korean actors,
Jasper Sleet, Coral Sleet, where AI enables sustained large-scale
misuse of legitimate access through things like
identity fabrication, through social engineering, and really
long-term persistence at very low cost.
We've also observed early threat actor experimentation
with agentic AI, where models are supporting era of decision
and task execution.
And there are many examples from our ecosystem on this as well.
Anthropic, for example, reported how Claude was used
as part of an attack workflow where it performed
80 to 90 percent of the operational tasks autonomously
without human direction.
For attackers, AI changes everything.
Now, the intent of a skilled operator is still required,
but AI is allowing an expert attacker to be
exponentially more effective.
That tells us something profound about the future of security.
It tells us that today's threats aren't
just faster, they're structurally different.
And in this new reality, security has to change.
For too long, we've relied on layers of siloed point
solutions, static policies, and human reliant response.
But attackers don't think in silos.
They think in graphs, and with agents, they can now operate
continuously at machine speed across these graphs.
What this means is that defenders,
we need to change our game.
We need to move at unprecedented scale,
speed, and sophistication.
It also means that as defenders, we have to think of
security comprehensively, because if you only have
security at specific control points, the attacker will just
find another way in.
At Microsoft, we believe the future of security is
ambient and autonomous.
Just like the AI, it needs to protect.
What I mean by that is that you can't simply turn on security.
It has to be something that's woven deeply into every layer
of the AI stack, from agents to apps, to platforms,
to infrastructure, to the silicon, everything.
It needs to be always on, always there, everywhere.
Security needs to go from reactive to proactive,
and it has to act safely, responsibly, and at the
scale of AI.
That is the future of security.
Now, to deliver on this, we need to use agents.
We need to use agents that are continuously discovering,
testing, and fixing the attack paths in an always-on
self-defending loop, so defenders can address these
attacks before they happen.
Imagine that.
Of course, humans stay in control.
We need to validate and we need to govern the actions of
these agents, and we need to make sure that security is
operating at the scale of AI.
And as we do this, I know that we will build trust at
the very core of our organizations, and security
becomes that incredible catalyst for innovation.
So let's talk about what this means in practice and what do
we need to do.
The first thing, to secure AI, we must start
with the foundations.
In the agentic age, you still need to secure the
foundations, human identities, data, endpoints, cloud, apps,
infrastructure, and you need to make sure that these
foundations are secure by design and by default.
Ambient and autonomous security at that foundational
level means that security is continuously embedded in
the environment itself.
Think across hardware and networks and sensors
and infrastructure, cloud facilities, all that.
So the system is always sensing, it's always reasoning,
it's adapting, rather than waiting for alerts and alarms.
Now, while we're securing these foundations,
what is rapidly changing today is that agents are
joining our workforce.
They're becoming our colleagues.
In fact, by 2028, IDC projects that there will be
1.3 billion agents, and we are already seeing organizations
scaling agents with 80 percent of Fortune 500 organizations
building and using agents.
Yet less than half of the organizations today report a
readiness for GenAI use, half.
Agents must be secured, and they must be secured with the
same vigilance that we use to secure people.
Otherwise, they risk what we call becoming double agents.
Sounds very sci-fi-ish.
But these agents can get manipulated by threat
actors and engage in nefarious actions.
We've seen examples of this.
It is important that we address things
like agents' fraud.
We protect data from leaking.
We are protecting these agents from external attacks
like prompt injections, and all the time we are
complying with regulations.
So where does this start?
First and foremost, it starts with observability,
because we cannot protect what we cannot see.
And in this era of agentic AI, organizations will need an
observability control plane.
Not just security teams, but IT teams, developer teams,
and security teams.
And all of these roles will need shared security controls
for agent identity, for threat protection,
for security posture, for data security and governance.
So let's start and take a look at each of these layers.
Let's start with identity.
For agent identity, it's imperative that AI
agents be treated as active participants.
They must be secured just like humans, with dynamic identity
based on behavior and context, managing least privileged
access, having policy bound controls across apps, clouds,
networks, users, and more.
To prevent these unsafe actions before execution,
we need to ensure that agents have access to only
what is needed, and we take that access off when it's not needed.
Let's go to threat protections.
We need threat protections that can learn and adapt.
Every agent will need to be continuously assessed for
risky permissions or misconfig, so we reduce that
exposure right up front.
Further, as these agents operate, we need to make sure
that we are monitoring their behavior in real-time,
inspecting their actions, and blocking suspicious activity
as it happens.
We also need to continuously correlate these signals across
the environment so that we can uncover stealthy or
novel techniques that others could miss.
That's super important.
These novel techniques, like jailbreaks and prompt
injections, require agentic security, because it needs
to operate continuously.
It needs to reason across all these signals
to detect intent, and it needs to act at machine speed.
Now, let's go to another critical part, which is data.
Because these agents work with data, we need to be able to see
how these agents interact with sensitive information,
what's going in, what's coming out.
We need to make sure that we're applying data loss
prevention policies, that we're applying sensitivity
labels in real time, and we are preventing oversharing and
leakage before it becomes a breach.
Governance, a very important thing, can no
longer be periodic, human-driven process.
It must be a continuous built-in system of guardrails.
And as autonomy increases, we need to make sure that
governance systems don't just observe behavior, but they act
within defined boundaries to prevent risks, to constrain
unsafe actions, and maintain alignment with
business intentions, as well as regulations all the
time with the human in the loop.
Now, finally, and very importantly, while the AI
is reducing the barrier for attackers everywhere,
we know that, it's also giving defenders
this incredible, powerful opportunity to tilt the skills.
With AI agents, we can see patterns,
we can respond faster, and with this, security shifts
from constant reaction to building resilience.
Bringing these agents into the workflow helps defenders do a
myriad of things, from triaging incidents,
to optimizing identity, conditional access policies,
surfacing and customizing that threat intelligence we need,
and maintaining secure compliant endpoints among
a few things.
I believe that agents will just simply become the
augmentation and the team for every single defender.
These agents are going to become a primary interface to
an organization security data, the logic and tools, and they
will need a comprehensive platform which helps them
access the data they need, learn, reason, and adapt,
enabling security to be deployed at scale, working 24/7
and traversing really complex databases, artefacts,
understanding any language, and doing all of this work in
a fraction of a second.
How cool is that?
Together, this vision shifts security from reacting and
reactive to a proactive and a predictive, continuously
self-defending system that operates at that agentic speed.
This is the future of security.
It is agentic security, where we are securing AI with AI.
Now, what we're talking about is a big step forward, no doubt.
But this is a critical one.
Can we get there?
Well, we must, and as always, we'll need to approach this
technology and AI evolution with great humility.
So here are a few things that we have learned.
In an environment of such rapid progress and change,
zero trust is critical and needs to extend to AI.
We need to have continuous verification,
least privileged access, and assume breach across identity,
data, and runtime behavior.
The second is that measurements and evaluations
are going to be critical to build trust
and progress towards autonomy.
It will be incumbent upon organizations to develop
their own evaluation and validation criteria.
AI agents need to earn the right to operate in your environment,
and that means, as security professionals,
we need to put them through the paces to see how accurate and
trustworthy they are.
We will need to understand the guardrails and safety measures
that matter most for our organizations to understand
which agents can run with some autonomy and which ones
need more oversight.
The third lesson is that security skillsets must
continue to evolve.
I know we feel this every single day.
Now, last year when I was on the stage, I shared my belief
that security professionals will need to learn to manage
agents as part of your security teams.
I still believe that's true, and that's happening.
But the difference between then and now is the speed
at which everything is moving, so fast.
And given that everyone can create an agent, no-code,
low-code tools, I think what's happening is these agents are
also becoming very capable of creating their own task agents.
So security professionals are going to have to not just
manage these agents, but really continuously validate
and evaluate them.
I think it's exciting.
The truth is, today, there's so much to learn.
And the much of the promise of AI depends really on humanity
coming together to ensure that AI serves a common good.
But our collective community is incredibly powerful.
By sharing information and best practices, we can better
understand how we need to evolve as defenders and how we
can better protect organizations and innovation
in the era of AI.
After all, in a connected world, security is a team sport.
That's why it's my great honor to introduce, via video,
a leader who has been a champion of initiatives
in emerging technologies, public-private partnerships,
and international collaboration, His Excellency
Dr. Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, Head of Cybersecurity for
the UAE Government Cybersecurity Council.
His Excellency was not able to travel here in-person,
but we wanted to share his story as his organization is setting
an incredible example of what the future of
security looks like.
Let's take a look.
>> MOHAMED AL KUWAIT: Greetings to you all from the UAE.
While I could not be with you in-person, especially that
I've been to every RSA in the past 15 years, I wanted my
voice to be presented in this great conference.
The UAE has set a national ambition to build
one billion AI agent.
These agents will span every sector from government services,
to financial services, to healthcare and beyond.
But we must be clear, every agent is also a new identity,
a new endpoint and a new surface that must be secured.
At the UAE Cybersecurity Council, we see this not only
as a challenge, but as a strategic opportunity.
Properly governed and secured, agent can
strengthen national resilience.
They can extend into roles such as cybersecurity analysts,
operating beyond human duty cycles, and supporting
continuous protection across the AI infrastructure that we
are building domestically.
This is an area where we are eager to explore further with
partners such as Microsoft to evaluate what is possible,
understand the implications, and determine together how
agents can operate safely and effectively at a national scale.
When a nation reaches that level of AI deployment,
the impact on capacity and productivity
can be unprecedented.
This is why we are pursuing what we call National XDR,
extended detection and response, not at the
enterprise level, but at the country level.
Imagine a unified capability that delivers visibility and
responds across critical sectors, powered by AI agents
that correlate threats, share intelligence, and take action
in real time.
No nation can defend in isolation.
That is why we have invested in Crystal Ball, our initiative
for international threat intelligence sharing.
Now we are developing Crystal Ball 2.0,
designed to scale collaboration across countries,
sectors, and communities.
The next evolution is clear.
We must move from human-to-human intelligence
sharing to agent-to-agent intelligence sharing.
Crystal Ball 2.0 is being designed with that vision,
enabling AI agent to exchange threat intelligence at machine
speed across borders so that when a threat is detected in
one nation, defensive action can be activated everywhere.
In closing, I'm happy and honored to be with you
all virtually, and we look forward to strengthening
collaboration with partners across governments, industries,
and the global cybersecurity community.
>> VASU JAKKAL: Well, many thanks to the UAE Government
Cybersecurity Council for demonstrating the future of
security in action.
35 years from now, when security professionals gather
in this place, what will the future look like?
With the pace of innovation today, it's every bit as
impossible for us to imagine what that future holds as it
would have been for RSAC attendees back in 1991.
But today, agentic AI is no longer fiction.
It is the most consequential technology of our time, and
security is the key to ensuring that agentic AI
is worthy of the trust we aspire to place in it.
We, in this room, hold the awesome opportunity and
responsibility to help shape the future, and at times,
it will be a struggle.
The most important work always is, but look around.
We're not alone.
This is a community, and we'll create the future
we want together.
Thank you so much.
